notes.meaning: Paul tells every Christian to live under the rulers over them. Government itself is God's idea, set up to keep order instead of chaos. Even a bad ruler has power only because God allows it, though God does not approve the wrong they do. Paul wrote this while Nero ruled Rome, and it applies to every form of government.

differ.view: Lutherans see government as God's 'left hand.' It rules by law and the sword to keep outward peace. It cannot make anyone right with God, and Christians live under it to serve their neighbour.
Some Baptist teachers speak of 'two ages' rather than two kingdoms. Rulers are honoured because their sword keeps order and makes room for the gospel, not because they can save anyone.

notes.meaning: Government is God's arrangement, so fighting against it means fighting against God. Those who do will bring judgment on themselves. Here that word means punishment, from the ruler and from God too. Paul means rebelling against lawful order. He does not mean we must obey a command to sin.

differ.view: Private people should not take authority away from rulers God has set over them. Christians must disobey when the state commands what God forbids. Even so, they should not deal with corrupt rulers outside the law.

Wesley forbade resisting rulers 'in any other manner than the laws of the community direct.' That leaves room to oppose them by lawful means. Methodist commentator Adam Clarke held that a ruler who overturns the nation's laws may be lawfully removed.

notes.meaning: Paul speaks of rulers in general and of what God meant them to be. Their job is to hold back wrongdoers, not to frighten good people. Those who live honestly can usually expect protection and even approval. Paul knew some rulers persecute the good, but he is describing the purpose God gave them.

A ruler is God's servant, appointed for the people's good. Christians must not take revenge themselves (12:19), but God brings justice through rulers. The 'sword' stands for the power to punish, even with death. Rulers answer to God and must serve the public, not themselves.

Christians should submit for two reasons. One is to avoid punishment. The deeper reason is conscience, because obeying rulers is part of obeying God. But if rulers command something sinful, we must obey God rather than people.

This is why Christians pay taxes. Running a government takes time and money, and officials give themselves to the work. Paying taxes honours God's arrangement. Taxes are meant for keeping order and protecting people, not for rulers' private pleasures.

Paul sums up what we owe rulers: taxes on people and property, fees on goods, respect and honour. 'Respect' here means reverence and obedience, not terror. Christians should pay these honestly, as a real debt, without cheating. Even when a person in office is unworthy, we can still respect the office.

From debts owed to rulers, Paul turns to debts in general: pay what you owe and don't leave bills unpaid. This does not forbid all borrowing, but it warns against careless debt and failing to repay. Love is the one debt we can never finish paying. Loving others keeps all God's commands about our neighbour.

Paul lists commands about how we treat others: do not commit adultery, murder, steal or covet. All of them are summed up in 'Love your neighbour as yourself,' from Leviticus 19:18, which Jesus repeated. We should love our neighbour as sincerely as we love ourselves. A heart full of love keeps these commands without needing to think about each one.

Love never harms a neighbour. It stops us from doing wrong, and it also moves us to do good. That is why love fulfils the law: it meets all that God's law asks about our neighbour. No one loves perfectly, though, so we still rely on Christ's grace.

Paul gives another reason to live this way: know what time it is. It is time to wake up from spiritual laziness and carelessness. Each day brings believers closer to their final salvation, whether Christ returns or they die first. Being closer to the finish should make us more eager, not slower.

The 'night' is this present life with its sin and darkness. The 'day' is the full light of heaven and Christ's coming. As on any morning, we take off our night clothes, here our sinful deeds. Then we put on the 'armour of light': graces God gives, such as faith and hope, for Christians are soldiers.

Live decently, as people do in daylight when everyone can see. Paul names three pairs of sins: wild parties and drunkenness, sexual sin and shameless living, quarrelling and jealousy. These sins often go together. Christians should live as if all they do is seen, because God sees it.

Instead, 'put on' the Lord Jesus Christ like clothing. This means being joined to him, following his example, and being made strong by his Spirit to live a holy life. Some older teachers also see here being covered by Christ's goodness, which makes us right with God. We should meet our body's real needs, but not plan ways to feed sinful desires.
